summary: A landlocked grand duchy in Western Europe, small in area but among the highest in the world in per capita income. It is one of the founding members of the European Union and a major center of finance and EU institutions.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: After Saint Willibrord founded an abbey at Echternach in the 7th century, Catholicism took root in Luxembourg. During the Reformation Luxembourg was under the rule of Spain and then the Austrian Habsburgs, and it strictly maintained the Catholic faith. Catholicism has long been bound up with Luxembourg's national identity, festivals and education; the Diocese of Luxembourg was established in 1870 and raised to an archdiocese in 1988.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: After the war Luxembourg's economic prosperity and high level of education, together with urbanization driven by the steel and finance industries, led to a rapid rise in secularization. In 2015 the government and religious groups agreed to abolish religious instruction in schools and replace it with a "Life and Society" course, reflecting a change in social attitudes toward religion; young people in particular often have no religious affiliation.

ranking.name: Other Christianity (Protestant, Orthodox, etc.)
ranking.description: Protestants are mostly immigrants who moved from Germany after the 19th century and foreign nationals working in EU institutions, while Orthodox Christians are mostly immigrants from Greece, Serbia and Russia. As the seat of EU institutions and an international financial center, Luxembourg has attracted many foreigners, and religion has diversified accordingly.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Muslims are mainly Bosnians and Montenegrins who fled to Luxembourg during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, along with North African and Turkish immigrants. In 2015 the government formally recognized Islam and signed an agreement with Muslim organizations.

religion.background: Luxembourg accepted Christianity in the late Roman period. In the 7th century Saint Willibrord founded an abbey in nearby Echternach to spread Christianity, and the "Dancing Procession" there still commemorates him today. In the Middle Ages Luxembourg belonged to the Holy Roman Empire, and after the Reformation it remained Catholic under the rule of Spain and then the Austrian Habsburgs. It became a grand duchy after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and was neutralized in 1867. Luxembourg long practiced cooperation between church and state, with the government paying the salaries of clergy; in 2015 the government signed an agreement with religious groups to abolish religious instruction in schools and reform church funding, moving toward the separation of church and state.

language.official: The official languages are Luxembourgish (national language), French and German.

ranking.name: Luxembourgish
ranking.description: Luxembourgish developed from the medieval Moselle Franconian dialect. During World War II the Nazis attempted to Germanize Luxembourg, and Luxembourgers took Luxembourgish as a symbol of their national identity. It was made the national language in 1984. Since foreigners make up nearly half the population, only about half of people speak Luxembourgish as their main language, but it is a language test that must be passed to obtain citizenship.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: In the 1960s–70s Luxembourg's steel and construction industries recruited large numbers of Portuguese workers, and the Portuguese gradually became the largest foreign community, making up about 15 percent of the total population. Portuguese is therefore very common in daily life in Luxembourg, and many schools also offer Portuguese courses.

ranking.name: French
ranking.description: French has been the language of the Luxembourg nobility and administration since the Middle Ages, and after independence in 1839 French became the language of legislation; laws are still written in French today. In addition, large numbers of cross-border commuters come every day from France and Belgium, making French the common language of the workplace and business.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: Luxembourg is the seat of EU institutions such as the Court of Justice of the European Union and the European Investment Bank, and is also an international financial center, attracting many English-speaking professionals. English is widely used in finance and international institutions, and those whose main language is English make up a small part of the population.

ranking.name: German
ranking.description: German was the main language of instruction in Luxembourg's schools in the 19th and 20th centuries, and newspapers and media were also mostly written in German. Today students first learn reading and writing in German in primary school, but those whose main language is German are mainly immigrants from Germany and cross-border commuters.

language.history: Luxembourgish derives from the Franconian dialect of the medieval Moselle valley, is closely related to German, and was long regarded as a dialect of German. After Luxembourg became independent in 1839, French and German became the administrative languages, with French the language of the elite and the law. During the Nazi occupation in 1941 a census was conducted, and the great majority refused to enter German as their mother tongue, so Luxembourgish became a symbol of resistance. In 1984 a law formally made Luxembourgish the national language, alongside French and German as administrative languages; in school education the three languages are learned in turn, making most people multilingual.

ranking.name: Judd mat Gaardebounen (smoked pork collar with broad beans)
ranking.description: Salt-cured, smoked pork collar stewed together with broad beans and potatoes and topped with a cream sauce, regarded as the national dish. It is salty and savory, with the aroma of smoked meat and broad beans complementing each other.
ranking.history: Judd mat Gaardebounen is a traditional Luxembourg farmhouse dish that uses smoked pork and broad beans harvested in summer, reflecting the produce of the Luxembourg countryside and the tradition of preserving meat. It is Luxembourg's most representative dish, often appearing at summer festivals and family gatherings, and Luxembourgers also use it as a representative dish to express national identity.

ranking.name: Gromperekichelcher (potato pancakes)
ranking.description: Grated potatoes mixed with onion, egg and flour and deep-fried into pancakes, often eaten with applesauce. With a golden, crisp exterior, they are a common hot snack at festival markets.
ranking.history: After the 18th century potatoes became the staple of Luxembourg farm families, and Gromperekichelcher (meaning "little potato cakes") is a common home-style dish. It is a representative snack at festival markets and Christmas markets across Luxembourg, and especially in the cold of winter, people buy a steaming hot portion of potato fritters from outdoor stalls.

ranking.name: Bouneschlupp (green bean soup)
ranking.description: A thick soup cooked from green beans, potatoes, onion and bacon or sausage. It has a thick texture with the aroma of smoked meat and green beans, and is a home-style winter soup.
ranking.history: Bouneschlupp is a traditional Luxembourg home-style soup, originating as a simple dish that farm families made with green beans from their own vegetable gardens. In the past it was an important staple for rural families in winter, with smoked meat added for flavor. Today it remains Luxembourgers' representative soup for the cold season and is also regarded as one of the symbols of Luxembourg's food culture.

ranking.name: Kachkéis (cooked cheese)
ranking.description: A soft cheese made from fermented milk, heated until melted into a spreadable, thick cheese cream, often spread on bread. It has a smooth texture and a distinctive fermented aroma.
ranking.history: Kachkéis is a distinctive Luxembourg dairy product, originating from farm families using surplus milk to make cheese that could be kept for a long time. Its production requires the cheese to ferment for several days before being heated and melted, giving it a unique aroma. Traditionally it was the breakfast and snack of farm families, and today it is a local specialty that Luxembourgers take pride in.

ranking.name: Quetschentaart (plum tart)
ranking.description: A fruit tart made with a yeast dough or pastry base, topped with halved plums and baked. The sweet-and-tart plum juice soaks into the crust, and it is often sprinkled with sugar or eaten with cream.
ranking.history: Quetschentaart is a seasonal dessert of late summer and early autumn in Luxembourg, when the plums of the Moselle valley are harvested. Around September many village festivals and markets sell plum tarts, and families also bake large quantities during the season to share with relatives and friends. This dessert reflects the seasonality of Luxembourg agriculture and rural traditions.
